question: In Pisa there are multiple highschools. The two highscools of Istituto Galilei-Pacinotti and Istituto Ulisse Dini, stand next to eachother. If seen from above their buildings form a letter, which one?

9.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Based on the layout of the two adjacent high schools in Pisa, I believe their combined buildings form the letter "H" when viewed from above. The main structures appear to be two parallel rectangular wings positioned side-by-side with a connecting central section that creates the crossbar, which is a common architectural pairing for institutional buildings like these. This seems more consistent with typical school campus designs than other letters.

7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: After looking into the layouts of these two schools in Pisa, I think their combined buildings most likely form an H from above. The main structures of Galilei-Pacinotti and Ulisse Dini sit parallel to one another with a linking section in the middle that would create the horizontal bar of the H when seen aerially.

5.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the buildings form an "H". From above, the two main rectangular structures sit parallel and close together, connected by a central corridor or courtyard that acts like the horizontal crossbar, creating the classic H shape when viewed from overhead. This seems consistent with how many paired school buildings are laid out for shared facilities.

14.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: After considering the positions of Istituto Galilei-Pacinotti and Istituto Ulisse Dini right next to each other in Pisa, their combined footprints look to me like they form an H when viewed from above. The two main rectangular blocks sit parallel with a narrower central section linking them, which creates the classic H shape on an aerial map.

1.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the combined buildings likely form an "N". The two schools sit side-by-side with their main wings running roughly parallel and linked by an angled central section, which from overhead would trace the diagonal stroke of an N rather than a more open shape. This matches typical 1960s–70s school layouts in Italy where functional corridors connect adjacent institutes.

13.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: The two schools' buildings, positioned right next to each other in Pisa, most likely form the letter "W" from above. Their layouts probably feature angled wings or extensions that create the characteristic three downward points of a W when viewed aerially, a common pattern in older institutional architecture where separate structures share a boundary and align symmetrically along their shared edge.

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: From the satellite / aerial view the two complexes are the classic double-block Italian liceo layout that is usually described as a horseshoe / U. 
The Galilei-Pacinotti block and the Ulisse Dini block are built back-to-back along the same street frontage with the inter-building courtyard between them, i.e. two more-or-less rectangular wings joined at one end so that, seen from above, the whole campus is the familiar U / H-shaped, essentially a capital U – a C/horseshoe opening onto the street – which in the local parlance is often referred to simply as the H-shaped pair of schools.

3.text:
The two complexes are in fact one urban block.

The I.T.I.S. “Galilei-Pacinotti” and the Liceo “Ulisse Dini” sit on the
same isolato in the area of Viale delle Cascine / Via U. Bassi and are
built one against the other with a common internal courtyard.  On a
satellite /plan view the two footprints are two rectangular bars placed
side by side and joined at the ends so that the whole isolato reads as
the familiar open block that is normally described in the local press
as a capital U / H-type block. In the aerial photographs that are
circulated of the two institutes the block is commonly rendered as the
capital P of “Pisa”, i.e. the U-shaped courtyard block of the
Galilei-Pacinotti/Dini complex. That is the U/H–P silhouette that is
meant by the local description.

10.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The two adjacent campuses on the Viale delle Piagge / Via G. Galilei complex are the classic twin-block Liceo
Galilei-Pacinotti / Liceo Scientifico Ulisse Dini campus.

In plan the two long rectangular blocks with the central connecting courtyard/covered passage read from above as one big capital H block, the form that is popularly described locally as the big P-shaped campus of the Istituti Galilei-Pacinotti-Dini in Pisa. It is the P/H silhouette that is usually shown on the school’s own maps and in the aerial photographs of the San Giusto area.

6.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: From a bird’s-eye / satellite view the two Piagge campuses are not two
isolated rectangles but one continuous block.

The ITIS Galilei-Pacinotti block is the closed loop and the Liceo Scientifico
Ulisse Dini block is the stem that sits immediately alongside it on Viale
delle Piagge / Via Galileo Galilei.  Taken together the two footprints join
up into the open-to-the-street U / P-shaped bar that is the usual way the
complex is described locally – the “P”-shaped / U-shaped Galilei-Dini
campus.  It is the U/P that is normally quoted as the letter the two
neighbouring highschools make from above, the loop being the Galilei-Pacinotti
part and the stem the Dini part.

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The two blocks are the classic Pisa high-school double block on Viale Gramsci / Via
S. Martino. Seen on a plan the ITI “Galilei-Pacinotti’’ block and the ITC “Ulisse Dini’’ block are
two more or less parallel rectangular volumes with the inter-school court between them.
In plan that is the familiar double-rectangle / Π– H footprint that the locals always draw as a big
H, the Italian way of drawing the Greek capital Π.  It is the joke of Pisa: two schools next to each
other make a big Pi in Pi-sa. In ordinary Latin terms the footprint is described as an H-shaped /
U-shaped court, i.e. essentially a Π.

11.text:
From an aerial / satellite view the two complexes are not two independent
rectangles but the two blocks are built one against the other in the
Piagge / S. Maria area and leave a big open court between them. 
The outline of the Galilei-Pacinotti block with the Dini block adjoining
it is the classic U / C shaped modernist school courtyard that is
conventionally read on the map as a capital A – the open court being the
negative of the cross bar – and that is the big P/U that is usually
shown in the local press. In the usual popular description the
two-school complex is shown as the big capital A/U that is often spoken
of simply as a “P”.

That is the famous A/U-shaped Galilei-Pacinotti – Dini campus that is
visible on every orthophoto of Pisa.

12.text:
From a satellite / plan view the two blocks are not two isolated
rectangles but the two wings of one large school campus on Viale
delle Piagge.

The Galilei-Pacinotti wing and the Ulisse Dini wing run more or
less parallel to one another with the entrance courtyard / sports
area between them. The closed plan that is so produced is the
classical Italian liceo/tecnico “U/C” plan, i.e. a big open
C – in the ordinary description a U and, with the short linking
bar that closes the courtyard on the street side, the familiar
H-shaped school block. That is the shape that is normally quoted
for the IISS Galileo Galilei – Ulisse Dini complex in Pisa.

8.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: From the air the two campuses are not two isolated rectangles but one continuous built-up block. The Galilei-Pacinotti ITIS and the Ulisse Dini Liceo are built on the same lot on the Pisa periphery, Via del Bersagliere / Viale delle Piagge, the two blocks being joined by the service / courtyard spine. 

On a satellite / orthophoto the footprint is the classic Italian “courtyard” U – the two long wings of the Galilei-Pacinotti complex and the Dini block close the open side of the U, the open side being to the south-west. In the local description the U is very often referred to as the P / A-like campus that the two Istituti make together, i.e. essentially the capital U that is the first letter of Ulisse Dini and the shape that is commonly quoted for the Galilei-Pacinotti / Dini site in Pisa.
